questions.q: What is the difference between `Mono` and `Flux` in Project Reactor?
o: `Mono` emits zero or one item, `Flux` zero to many
`Mono` is synchronous, `Flux` is asynchronous
`Mono` is for numbers, `Flux` is for strings
`Flux` can only emit a fixed number of items
questions.w: Both are lazy publishers. Nothing happens until something subscribes.

questions.q: You build a `Flux` pipeline but nothing happens. What is the most likely cause?
o: Nobody has subscribed to it
The pipeline has too many operators
Reactor needs to be restarted
The Flux has been marked read-only
questions.w: Reactive streams are lazy. In WebFlux the framework subscribes for you when you return the `Mono` or `Flux` from a handler.

o: The subscriber tells the publisher how many items it can take
A lock that is held on a single database row until commit
A cache eviction policy that removes the oldest entries first
A way of compressing messages before they cross the network
questions.w: Subscribers request items with `request(n)`. Operators such as `onBackpressureBuffer` and `onBackpressureDrop` define what happens when demand is exceeded.

questions.q: A WebFlux handler calls a blocking JDBC query on the event loop thread. What is the effect?
o: It blocks one of a few event-loop threads, so throughput can collapse
Nothing happens, because the framework unblocks the call for you
The query runs faster than usual because Netty tunes it
Netty retries the blocked call automatically on another thread
questions.w: Use a non-blocking driver (R2DBC) or move blocking work to `Schedulers.boundedElastic()`. BlockHound can detect such calls in tests.

questions.q: When is WebFlux a good fit?
o: Many concurrent I/O-bound connections with non-blocking dependencies
Heavy CPU-bound computation that keeps every core busy
Applications that talk to the database only through JDBC and JPA
Small apps whose team only knows how to write blocking code
questions.w: Reactive code needs reactive dependencies end to end and a different mindset. For simple blocking stacks, Spring MVC (possibly with virtual threads) is easier.

questions.q: What does `flatMap` do compared with `map` on a `Flux`?
o: `flatMap` turns each item into a publisher and merges them
`flatMap` filters the items while `map` sorts all the items
`flatMap` blocks the thread while `map` never blocks at all
The two operators are identical and can be swapped freely
questions.w: Use `flatMap` when the transformation itself is asynchronous, such as a non-blocking call returning a `Mono`.

questions.q: How do Java 21 virtual threads compare with reactive programming?
o: They let blocking-style code scale without reactive operators
They replace the JVM itself with a lighter runtime
They only work when the application is also using Kafka
They move the code from the CPU onto the GPU for speed
questions.w: Both address thread-per-request limits. Virtual threads keep simple imperative code, while reactive adds streaming and backpressure semantics.

questions.q: How do you handle an error in a reactive chain?
o: Operators like `onErrorResume`, `onErrorReturn` or `retryWhen`
A `try/catch` around the whole pipeline
Nothing, because Reactor retries by default
Throw the error from `subscribe()` only
questions.w: Errors are signals in the stream. A `try/catch` around the assembly code will not see failures that happen later during execution.
